title: Combining out-of-order execution with high clock frequency (departure from the 21164)
where_in_paper: Introduction / design-approach discussion (performance framed as clock frequency × IPC, contrasted against earlier Alpha processors)
decision: Build the 21264 as an out-of-order, speculative machine with a large instruction window while preserving the Alpha emphasis on very high clock frequency, explicitly departing from the 21164's in-order, frequency-led design.
alternatives_or_rejected: The implicit alternative was continuing the 21164's in-order, statically scheduled approach, which obtained performance almost entirely from clock rate. I do not recall the paper enumerating a formal list of rejected designs; the frequency-vs-IPC contrast with earlier Alphas is how the trade-off is presented.
rationale: The paper argues that an in-order machine could not deliver the instructions-per-cycle improvement needed for the performance targets, and that the perceived conflict between out-of-order complexity and high frequency could be resolved by microarchitectural structuring (distributed queues, clustered execution) rather than by sacrificing one goal for the other.
outcome: The paper presents this as the central reason the 21264 roughly doubles the 21164's integer performance at comparable frequencies, and treats it as evidence that out-of-order execution and high frequency can coexist.

title: Hybrid branch predictor: local + global components with a chooser (over 35K bits of state)
decision: Use a combined predictor: a local-history component (roughly 1024 entries of 10-bit local histories feeding a 1024 × 3-bit local predictor), a global-history component (12-bit history into a 4096 × 2-bit predictor), and a 4096 × 2-bit chooser selecting between them — together more than 35,000 bits of prediction state.
alternatives_or_rejected: Simpler single-component predictors (e.g., bimodal or global-history-only) are the implicit baseline; I do not recall the paper explicitly listing rejected alternatives, it mainly justifies the hybrid on accuracy grounds. Exact table sizes are recalled with moderate confidence.
rationale: Local history captures branch-specific behavior, global history captures correlated branches, and the chooser picks the currently more reliable component; the deep out-of-order pipeline makes mispredictions expensive, justifying the large hybrid structure.
outcome: The paper credits this predictor with high accuracy on its benchmark workloads; I do not recall the exact misprediction figures quoted.

title: Two integer clusters with duplicated register files and per-cluster issue queues
where_in_paper: Instruction issue / integer execution unit section
decision: Organize the four integer pipelines into two clusters, each with its own 20-entry issue queue and a full duplicate copy of the 80-entry integer register file; each queue arbitrates oldest-ready among instructions assigned to its cluster, with results broadcast between clusters and an extra forwarding delay for cross-cluster dependences.
alternatives_or_rejected: The implicit alternative is a single centralized queue and one large, heavily multi-ported register file. I believe the paper motivates the duplication via port count, wiring, and cycle-time concerns, but I am not certain it explicitly presents the monolithic design as a considered-and-rejected option.
rationale: A centrally shared register file serving four issue pipelines would need many read/write ports and long wires, hurting cycle time; duplicating the file lets each cluster read operands locally and keeps each 20-entry queue's arbitration logic small and fast.
outcome: The design sustains up to four integer instructions issued per cycle at the target clock; the paper notes the cross-cluster forwarding penalty as a cost of this organization.

title: Register renaming into enlarged physical register files (80 integer / 72 FP)
decision: Rename into pools of 80 integer and 72 floating-point physical registers (versus 31 architectural of each), holding speculative results in the register files themselves; with the 20-entry fetch queue and the issue queues this yields roughly 80 instructions in flight. I recall misprediction recovery relying on checkpointing/copying of the rename map, with moderate confidence.
alternatives_or_rejected: A reorder-buffer-based renaming scheme is the natural alternative, but I do not recall the paper explicitly discussing or rejecting it; the 80/72 numbers and the physical-register-file approach are what I am actually confident about.
rationale: A large pool of rename registers is needed to keep the big out-of-order window busy; buffering results in the register files avoids a separate ROB data path (this framing is partly my inference).
outcome: The paper reports that the large window supplies enough in-flight state for the out-of-order engine to expose ILP, a key contributor to the performance gains over the 21164.

title: Large on-chip L1 caches with the second-level cache moved off-chip
decision: Provide 64 KB, two-way set-associative L1 instruction and data caches on-chip (the D-cache byte-writable and write-back, using the 'cloaking' mechanism for partial-line writes, recalled with moderate confidence), and place the multi-megabyte L2 off-chip (direct-mapped, sized roughly 1–16 MB, recalled with moderate confidence).
alternatives_or_rejected: The 21164's organization — small L1 plus a ~96 KB on-chip secondary cache — is the contrast case. I recall the trade-off being die area spent on the large L1s and the out-of-order core versus on an on-chip L2, but I am not certain how explicitly the paper frames the on-chip L2 as a considered-and-rejected option.
rationale: The out-of-order core needs substantially more first-level capacity and bandwidth than the 21164's caches provided; the L1s were enlarged accordingly, with the large off-chip L2 preserving capacity at modest die cost.
outcome: The paper reports the resulting hierarchy sustains the bandwidth and miss behavior the core needs, with notably strong performance on memory-intensive floating-point workloads.
